[id=p5.1] Mapping Gemma3 onto an Edge Dataflow Architecture
[id=p6.1] Shouyu Du * 1
Miaoxiang Yu * 1
Zhiheng Ni 1
Jillian Cai 1
Qing Yang 2
Tao Wei 1
Zhenyu Xu 1
††footnotetext: *Equal contribution
1Electrical and Computer Engineering, Clemson University, USA
2Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Rhode Island, USA.
Correspondence to: Zhenyu Xu <zxu3@clemson.edu>, Tao Wei <twei2@clemson.edu>.
Abstract
[id=abstract1.1] We present the first end-to-end deployment of the Gemma3 family of large language and vision models on a tiled edge dataflow architecture (AMD Ryzen AI NPU). Our work introduces a set of hardware-aware techniques. For prefill, we introduce an efficient dequantization engine, optimize tiled matrix multiplication kernels, and propose FlowQKV, a chunked, pipelined attention mechanism. For decoding, we introduce FusedDQP, which fuses dequantization and projection into a single kernel, and FlowKV, which re-structures attention to sustain high memory bandwidth utilization. Together with a compact Q4NX 4-bit quantization format, these methods yield up to 5.2×5.2\times faster prefill and 4.8×4.8\times faster decoding versus the iGPU, and 33.5×33.5\times and 2.2×2.2\times over the CPU, respectively. Power efficiency improves by as much as 67.2×67.2\times and 222.9×222.9\times compared to the iGPU and CPU. The proposed approach demonstrates that modern NPUs can deliver practical, low-power LLM and VLM inference at the edge, and provides a generalizable blueprint for mapping transformer-based models onto tiled dataflow accelerators.
[id=S1]
1 Introduction
[id=S1.p1.1] Local LLMs are rising for latency, offline use, and privacy: on-device inference keeps sensitive data local and avoids network delays needed for real-time apps Exxact Corporation (2025). CPUs and iGPUs can be monopolized by LLM workloads, so NPUs—dedicated AI accelerators—run these tasks without degrading general-purpose performance Hunhoff et al. (2025). Major vendors (AMD, Intel, Apple, Qualcomm) now ship neural processing units (NPUs) Laptop Mag Editors (2024); Microsoft (2024). AMD’s Ryzen AI NPUs use XDNA: a 2D array of AI Engine tiles forming a dataflow chip with very-long-instruction-word (VLIW) compute; their flexible data-movement fabric enables direct tile-to-tile communication, easing internal bandwidth bottlenecks and improving speed and power efficiency Rico and others (2024); Rosti and Franz (2025); AMD/Xilinx (2025); Hunhoff et al. (2025); Zhuang et al. (2025); Xu et al. (2025b); Xu et al. (2025a).
[id=S1.p2.1] However, a full end-to-end deployment of Gemma3 models (vision) on AMD Ryzen AI NPUs has not yet been demonstrated Google DeepMind (2025). We present the first demonstration; and since Gemma3 is both representative and popular, the resulting insights offer a practical blueprint for subsequent model deployment and runtime designs.
[id=S1.p3.1] LLM inference consists of two distinct phases: prefill and decoding. During prefill, the model reads the whole prompt once, stores the results as key–value (KV) cache, and–if it’s a multi-turn chat–adds these results to what was cached before, as well as image tokens (if any). This stage is compute-intensive. In contrast, decoding phase proceeds autoregressively, generating one token at a time. Each new token depends on the KV cache and previous outputs, which prevents parallelization and makes decoding memory-bound. For vision–language models (VLMs), Gemma3 incorporates a vision tower that converts an input image into 4096 tokens, which then compressed into 256 tokens, which are then processed together with text tokens during prefill.
[id=S1.p4.1] To accelerate prefill, we introduce a series of new techniques. First, we design an efficient dequantization engine that converts quantized projection layer weights into full precision (bf16). Second, we adopt a systematic, metric-driven approach to optimize tiled matrix multiplications (MMs) in bf16. Third, we propose FlowQKV, a novel technique designed for prefill. By exploiting dataflow, pipelining and bandwidth-aware scheduling, FlowQKV overlaps data movement with computation across multiple compute tiles (CTs), significantly improving KV cache efficiency and minimizing memory bottlenecks. One variant, FlowQKV-SWA is introduced to address Sliding Window Attention (SWA) in Gemma3. In addition, we introduce Q4NX (Quantized 4-bit NPU eXpress), a compact and NPU-friendly data format that is specifically tailored to reduce memory footprint and maximize throughput on Ryzen AI NPUs. Collectively, the optimized MM kernels, FlowQKV, and Q4NX achieve sustained high memory bandwidth utilization.
[id=S1.p5.1] The vision tower benefits from many of the same optimizations applied to prefill. Another FlowQKV variant, FlowQKV-NCA (Non-Causal Attention), is introduced.
[id=S1.p6.1] For decoding, we propose two complementary methods. The first, FusedDQP, fuses dequantization and projection into a single kernel, effectively combining them into matrix–vector multiplications (MVMs). The second, FlowKV, restructures the attention mechanism into a dataflow model, optimizing the handling of key–value pairs. As in prefill, a FlowKV-SWA variant supports efficient deployment of SWA layers. Together, FusedDQP and FlowKV maintain consistently high memory bandwidth utilization (Umemr​dU_{\text{mem}}^{rd}) during decoding, thereby improving latency and throughput.
[id=S1.p7.1] We evaluate 4-bit quantized Gemma3 models (1B and 4B) on an AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 NPU. Using the same platform’s iGPU and CPU as baselines, the NPU achieves, for prefill, up to 5.2×5.2\times over the iGPU and 33.5×33.5\times over the CPU. For decoding—especially at longer sequences—the NPU matches or exceeds both baselines, reaching up to 4.8×4.8\times over the iGPU and 2.2×2.2\times over the CPU. For the vision tower (processing and understanding; 4B only), the NPU is 1.7×1.7\times faster than the iGPU and 8.7×8.7\times faster than the CPU. Importantly, the NPU demonstrates markedly superior energy efficiency—achieving up to 67.2×67.2\times and 222.9×222.9\times improvements over the iGPU and CPU, respectively, as measured in Tokens Per Second per Watt (TPS/W).
[id=S1.p8.1] Main contributions of this work are as follows:
[id=S1.I1.i1] •
[id=S1.I1.i1.p1.1] We present the first end-to-end deployment of Gemma3 models on an edge dataflow architecture.
[id=S1.I1.i2] •
[id=S1.I1.i2.p1.1] We propose a set of novel techniques to enable efficient prefill, decoding, and vision-tower execution.
[id=S1.I1.i3] •
[id=S1.I1.i3.p1.1] We share the lessons learned from this deployment, highlighting opportunities and challenges.
[id=S2]
2 Background
[id=S2.p1.1] This section briefs the computer architecture of the Ryzen AI NPU and model architecture of Gemma3.
[id=S2.SS1]
2.1 AMD Ryzen AI NPU Architecture
[id=S2.SS1.SSS1]
2.1.1 Platform Overview
[id=S2.SS1.SSS1.p1.1] The AMD Ryzen AI NPU architecture is built around interconnected 2D processing units Rico and others (2024). Exemplified by the NPU2 (XDNA2), these units are referred to as Compute Tiles (CTs). It features a 32-CT grid (8 columns and each contains 4 CTs) in a checkerboard layout, shown in Fig. 1. These instructions are dispatched across two parallel processors: the scalar processor, which handles complex pointer arithmetic, and the vector processor, which is optimized for SIMD (Single Instruction Multiple Data) operations. Each CT runs at a clock speed up to 1.8 GHz.
Figure 1: NPU architecture overview
[id=S2.SS1.SSS2]
2.1.2 Compute Tiles (CTs)
[id=S2.SS1.SSS2.p1.1] The vector processor supports both floating-point and fixed-point operations. Integrated pre-add units handle basic vector functions such as minimum/maximum calculations and direct vector comparisons. CT local data memory (DM), also referred to as L1 memory, is divided into eight banks (a total of 64 KB), each accessible via a DMA (Direct Memory Access) interface, shown in Fig. 2.
[id=S2.SS1.SSS2.p2.1] CTs communicate through two primary interfaces. The first is AIE (AI Engine) memory access, enabling direct load/store operations between neighboring CTs. The second is the AXI4 (Advanced eXtensible Interface 4) interconnect, which allows DMA transfers to non-adjacent CTs via AXI4 streams. This interface also supports input broadcasting by duplicating data for multiple CTs.
Figure 2: CT overview
[id=S2.SS1.SSS3]
2.1.3 Memory Tiles (MTs) and Shim Tiles (STs)
[id=S2.SS1.SSS3.p1.1] The platform includes 8 Memory Tiles (MTs), positioned at the bottom of the CT array, shown in Fig. 1. Each tile contains 512 KB of high-density, high-bandwidth memory, also referred to as L2 memory. Shim Tiles (STs) provide communication with access to main memory (off-chip DDR memory). MT interfaces with ST to access main memory via AXI4 streams. Lightweight DMA engines within the MT and ST ensure efficient data transfer between the main memory and the CT array.
[id=S2.SS1.SSS4]
2.1.4 Programming
[id=S2.SS1.SSS4.p1.1] Programming the platform relies on two main components. Kernels are directly mapped to CTs to handle core computations, while the Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) manages connections and creates data buffers between tiles, facilitating efficient communication and coordination AMD/Xilinx (2025). These features collectively ensure scalability and the efficient execution of large-scale computations.
Figure 3: Data movement architecture on AMD NPU
[id=S2.SS1.SSS5]
2.1.5 Data Movement on NPU
[id=S2.SS1.SSS5.p1.1] The primary data transfers occur between main memory and L2, as well as between L2 and L1. Additionally, the architecture supports flexible interconnects, enabling direct transfers such as main memory to L1 and L1 to L1. A data transfer involves a source DMA channel (MM2S, or Memory-Mapped to Stream), a destination DMA channel (Steam to Memory-Mapped), and a configured stream interconnect connecting the two (see Fig. 3). The MM2S channel reads data from memory and places it on the stream, while the S2MM channel retrieves the data from the stream and writes it to memory. Each CT, MT, and ST is equipped with a stream interconnect switch and multiple MM2S and S2MM DMA channels (AXI4 interconnects). In the ST, DMA channels read and write to the main memory. Additionally, double buffering of input and output buffers in L1 memory allows data transfers to overlap with computation, effectively hiding data transfer latency.
[id=S2.SS2]
2.2 Model Architecture of Gemma3
[id=S2.SS2.SSS1]
2.2.1 Model Architecture
[id=S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.1] The model (text portion) consists of 34 transformer layers, with a pattern of 5 local layers (SWA with a window size of 1024) for every global layer (full attention), starting with a local layer as the first layer of the model Google DeepMind (2025); one representative layer is shown in Fig. 4, with dimensions and notation defined in the caption.
[id=S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.1] The vision tower is a 400M-parameter SigLIP Vision Transformer (ViT) Zhai et al. (2023). During preprocessing, each image is tokenized into 4,096 tokens, which are processed by 24 transformer layers (full, non-causal attention, no grouped query attention, or GQA). Functionally, this stage can be viewed as prefill, producing visual context (256 tokens per image) that seeds the language stack.
[id=S2.SS2.SSS1.p3.1] At a high level, the Gemma3 architecture (text and vision) comprises three operation classes: (i) projection operations / matrix multiplications (MM); (ii) attention computation—full or sliding-window (SWA), causal or non-causal—highlighted by the dotted red box in Fig. 4; and (iii) nonlinear functions such as RoPE, RMS normalization, GeLU, and QK-Norm.
Figure 4: Gemma3 4B model architecture (text portion; one transformer layer shown).
Key model parameters: D=2560D=2560 is the model dimension, H=8H=8 is the number of attention heads, and G=4G=4 is the number of KV groups.
The head dimension d=256d=256.
This dd is the dimensionality of each query (qq), key (kk), and value (vv) vector per head.
In prefill, LpL_{p} represents the sequence length (token length of the current prompt).
In decoding, Lp=1L_{p}=1.
LL represents the total sequence length, which increases progressively during autoregressive LLM inference (In local layer, the window length, LwL_{w}, for SWA is 1024).
The attention module (both full and SWA) is highlighted inside the dotted red box.
[id=S2.SS2.SSS2]
2.2.2 Projection Operation during Prefill–MM
[id=S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1] Projection weights 𝐖\mathbf{W} (e.g., 𝐖q\mathbf{W}_{q}, 𝐖k\mathbf{W}_{k}, 𝐖v\mathbf{W}_{v}, and 𝐖o\mathbf{W}_{o}) are applied to the input matrix. On edge devices, these weights are typically stored in low-precision formats–most commonly 4-bit integers (int4)–to alleviate off-chip memory capacity and memory bandwidth constraints. During prefill, the weights are first dequantized to full precision (bf16), and then transferred to the dedicated compute unit (e.g., NPU) to perform the MM operation. Note that in the vision tower, MM is handled similarly, except no quantization is used.
[id=S2.SS2.SSS3]
2.2.3 Attention Computation during Prefill
[id=S2.SS2.SSS3.p1.1] In the prefill phase, the model makes a single forward pass over the full prompt, stores the results as a KV cache, and–when it’s a multi-turn conversation–appends these results to the prior cache, as well as image tokens (if any). This passes through all layers (some are SWA in Gemma3, which lowers compute intensity). This prepares the model to generate the first output token, which then initiates the decoding phase.
[id=S2.SS2.SSS3.p2.1] To simplify the explanation, we consider a single-head attention mechanism and temporarily ignore GQA. Let LL denote the total context length, including both the previous tokens and the current prompt, and let LpL_{p} denote the number of tokens in the current prompt (i.e., the new input being prefed). We define the query matrix 𝐐∈ℝLp×d\mathbf{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{p}\times d}, the key matrix 𝐊∈ℝL×d\mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d}, and the value matrix 𝐕∈ℝL×d\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d}. The attention output matrix 𝐎∈ℝLp×d\mathbf{O}\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{p}\times d} is computed using the scaled dot-product attention formula:
[id=S2.E1]
𝐎=softmax​(𝐐𝐊⊤d)​𝐕\mathbf{O}=\text{softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}\right)\mathbf{V}
(1)
[id=S2.SS2.SSS3.p4.1] Here, the product 𝐐𝐊⊤∈ℝLp×L\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{p}\times L} contains the raw attention scores between each new query token and all tokens in the context. The softmax function is applied row-wise over the sequence length LL, producing a normalized attention weight matrix. The final output 𝐎\mathbf{O} is obtained by applying these attention weights to the value matrix 𝐕\mathbf{V}.
[id=S2.SS2.SSS3.p5.1] In Gemma3 (text portion), GQA is used, where each KV group is shared among H/GH/G query heads. H represents the number of attention heads and G represents the number of KV groups. As the conversation progresses and the total sequence length increases, the number of stored keys and values grows linearly with LL, resulting in increased memory access and compute demand. This makes attention computation the dominant performance bottleneck, particularly at long sequence lengths. Accordingly, Gemma-3 introduces local layers (via SWA) that attend only to the most recent LwL_{w} tokens. In addition, note that in the vision tower, attention is handled similarly, except it uses full non-causal attention.
[id=S2.SS2.SSS4]
2.2.4 Projection Operation during Decoding–MVM
[id=S2.SS2.SSS4.p1.1] During LLM decoding, the weights are first transferred to the compute unit, then dequantized back to bf16 precision before projection is performed. This introduces two distinct operations: dequantization and MVM. The separation of these steps incurs additional memory access and latency overhead, which becomes a performance bottleneck during projection. Addressing this inefficiency is critical for optimizing LLM decoding.
[id=S2.SS2.SSS5]
2.2.5 Attention Computation during Decoding
[id=S2.SS2.SSS5.p1.1] Shown in Eq. 2, the attention output at decoding step tt, denoted as 𝐨t∈ℝd\mathbf{o}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, is computed as a weighted sum over the value vectors 𝐯j∈ℝd\mathbf{v}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} from all previous time steps j=1j=1 to tt. Specifically, the attention weight for each position jj is determined by the dot product between the current query vector 𝐪t∈ℝd\mathbf{q}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and each key vector 𝐤j∈ℝd\mathbf{k}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, followed by softmax normalization over all previous positions. For simplicity, the scaling factor d\sqrt{d} is omitted here. This produces a probability distribution over prior tokens, reflecting their relative importance to the current token. The full attention computation is given by:
[id=S2.E2]
𝐨t=∑j=1texp⁡(𝐪t⊤​𝐤j)∑l=1texp⁡(𝐪t⊤​𝐤l)​𝐯j∈ℝd.\mathbf{o}_{t}=\sum_{j=1}^{t}\frac{\exp(\mathbf{q}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{k}_{j})}{\sum_{l=1}^{t}\exp(\mathbf{q}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{k}_{l})}\mathbf{v}_{j}\quad\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.
(2)
[id=S2.SS2.SSS5.p1.2] Here, dd denotes the dimension of each query, key, and value vector. Gemma3 uses GQA, where H/GH/G queries in a KV group share 1 KV group. As decoding proceeds, the number of stored keys and values increases linearly with tt, leading to growing memory access and compute requirements. This makes attention computation the primary performance bottleneck at longer sequence lengths. Note that in local layers, SWA is applied and the summation range in Eq. 2 is restricted to t−Lw+1​…​tt-L_{w}+1\ldots t when t>Lwt>L_{w} (otherwise 1​…​t1\ldots t).
[id=S2.SS2.SSS6]
2.2.6 Nonlinear functions
[id=S2.SS2.SSS6.p1.1] The computational cost of nonlinear functions in both prefill and decoding phases is comparatively low. Thus, our design will focus on projection and attention operations.
[id=S3]
3 Working Principles
[id=S3.SS1]
3.1 Prefill
[id=S3.SS1.p1.1] This section presents optimization techniques specifically designed for the NPU architecture.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS1]
3.1.1 Dequantization Engine
[id=S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1] Q4_1 quantization—using int4 weights and bf16 activations—is widely adopted for deploying LLMs on edge devices due to its favorable trade-off between model size and accuracy. Here, we use bf16 for all activations and non-projection weights in the proposed design. The dequantization logic is modular and format-agnostic, supporting schemes like Q4_1 or any block-wise quantization. In these schemes, weights are quantized in groups (e.g., size 32, 64, 128), each with a shared scale factor and minimal value offset, following:
[id=S3.E3]
w^i=dg⋅wq​i+mg\hat{w}_{i}=d_{g}\cdot w_{qi}+m_{g}
(3)
[id=S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.2] where wq​i∈{0,…,15}w_{qi}\in\{0,\dots,15\} is the int4 weight, dg∈ℝd_{g}\in\mathbb{R} is the scale, and mg∈ℝm_{g}\in\mathbb{R} is the minimal value offset of group gg.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS1.p2.1] We adopt group size g=32g=32, the minimum of commonly used group sizes, for best compatibility. As on AMD Ryzen AI NPU2, only bf16 precision multiplication is natively supported, all minimal value offsets are pre-converted to bf16 offline. To reduce on-chip memory usage, projection weights are tiled into blocks with a size of 32×25632\times 256. Each block stores 32×25632\times 256 int4 weights, 256256 bf16 scales, and 256256 bf16 minimal value offset, for a total size of 5,1205{,}120 bytes (5.05.0 KB). We refer to this compact format as Q4NX (Quantized 4-bit NPU eXpress). Note that Q4NX can be extended to support emerging MXFP4, making it future-proof.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS1.p3.1] Each CT processes a Q4NX block by dequantizing it using Eq. 3 and writing the full-precision result to DDR. Input (quantized) and output (dequantized) data are double-buffered to overlap computation and transfer.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS2]
3.1.2 Optimizing Projection Operations
[id=S3.SS1.SSS2.p1.1] In the prefill, all projection operations are implemented as MMs. This section begins by reviewing the fundamentals of tiling-based MM, followed by its mapping and implementation on AMD Ryzen AI NPUs. We then introduce performance metrics that guide the optimization process to improve compute efficiency and memory utilization.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS2.p2.1] Tiling-based MM is a well-established optimization technique for improving data locality and compute efficiency Goto and van de Geijn (2008). Consider the standard MM 𝐂=𝐀×𝐁\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}, where 𝐀∈ℝM×K\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times K}, 𝐁∈ℝK×N\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times N}, and 𝐂∈ℝM×N\mathbf{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times N} (Fig. 5). In the tiling-based approach, matrices 𝐀\mathbf{A} and 𝐁\mathbf{B} are partitioned into smaller submatrices (tiles) of dimensions m×km\times k and k×nk\times n, respectively. Each output tile 𝐜∈ℝm×n\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} is computed from the corresponding tiles 𝐚\mathbf{a} and 𝐛\mathbf{b}. Once all output tiles are computed and accumulated, the full matrix 𝐂\mathbf{C} is assembled. The total number of floating-point operations (multiply and add) required is 2⋅M⋅K⋅N2\cdot M\cdot K\cdot N. Assuming a single compute unit and ignoring reuse across tiles, the total data movement cost is approximately:
[id=S3.E4]
Nn⋅size​(𝐀)+Mm⋅size​(𝐁)\frac{N}{n}\cdot\text{size}(\mathbf{A})+\frac{M}{m}\cdot\text{size}(\mathbf{B})
(4)
[id=S3.SS1.SSS2.p2.2] This reflects the cost of loading the necessary tiles of 𝐀\mathbf{A} and 𝐁\mathbf{B} into local memory to compute all tiles of 𝐂\mathbf{C}.
Figure 5: Diagram of tiling-based MM. The concept of a supertile is specific to the AMD Ryzen AI NPU2 implementation and reflects the aggregated output block computed in K/kK/k load-compute cycles (2 in this example).
[id=S3.SS1.SSS2.p3.1] Efficient tiling-based MM on NPUs has been previously studied AMD/Xilinx (2025); Rosti and Franz (2025). In this approach, input matrices 𝐀\mathbf{A} and 𝐁\mathbf{B} are distributed to compute tiles (CTs) via DMA channels, as illustrated in Fig. 6. Specifically, tiles of 𝐀\mathbf{A} (denoted 𝐚\mathbf{a}) are broadcast to all CTs within a column, while tiles of 𝐁\mathbf{B} (denoted 𝐛\mathbf{b}) are broadcast to all CTs within a row.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS2.p4.1] The compute array is 8×48\times 4 CTs; each column receives a unique 𝐚\mathbf{a} tile and each row a unique 𝐛\mathbf{b} tile. Tiles load concurrently via DMA with double buffering to overlap transfer and compute, and the resulting 𝐜\mathbf{c} tiles are written back to DDR (write-back paths omitted).
Figure 6: Dataflow diagram of tiling-based MM on NPUs. Solid black arrows indicate the broadcast of tile 𝐚\mathbf{a} to all CTs within a column, while dotted black arrows represent the broadcast of tile 𝐛\mathbf{b} to all CTs within a row.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS2.p5.1] This dataflow computes an effective block of the output matrix 𝐂\mathbf{C} with dimensions 8​m×4​n8m\times 4n in K/kK/k load-and-compute cycles, shown in Fig. 5. We refer to this block as a supertile.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS2.p6.1] When the read memory bandwidth Umemr​dU^{rd}_{\text{mem}} is higher that the allocated memory bandwidth (memory-bound), we introduce a megatile, which is formed on the MT (L2). For example, if a supertile is sized 8​m×4​n8m\times 4n, then a megatile spans 8​ey⋅m×4​ex⋅n8e_{y}\cdot m\times 4e_{x}\cdot n, where exe_{x} and eye_{y} are expansion factors along the xx- and yy-axes, respectively. As a complete megatile (output CC block) surpasses the aggregate L1 memory capacity of the CTs, it must be staged and transferred out through the MTs (L2). The total data movement cost associated with megatile processing is given by:
[id=S3.E5]
N4​ex​n⋅size​(𝐀)+M8​ey​m⋅size​(𝐁)\frac{N}{4e_{x}n}\cdot\text{size}(\mathbf{A})+\frac{M}{8e_{y}m}\cdot\text{size}(\mathbf{B})
(5)

3.1.3 FlowQKV
[id=S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1] FlowQKV is a hardware-aware attention mechanism optimized for the prefill phase. It addresses the bandwidth bottleneck caused by full-sequence attention by restructuring how the model accesses and processes KV cache data. The method is explicitly designed to maximize DRAM bandwidth efficiency and enable pipelined execution across CTs.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS3.p2.1] During prefill, attention must use the current query matrix 𝐐\mathbf{Q} and all past KV cache entries accumulated across multiple conversation turns. This makes attention computation memory-intensive, especially for long sequences, as every query token must attend to all previous tokens. To address this, we apply a chunked processing strategy.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS3.p3.1] The input sequence is divided into fixed-size chunks of length LcL_{c}, and attention is computed incrementally across these chunks using a numerically stable accumulation scheme Milakov and Gimelshein (2018); Dao et al. (2022). Crucially, this approach preserves causal semantics: each query chunk attends to all key-value tokens up to and including the current chunk.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS3.p4.1] For chunked attention, let
𝐐c∈ℝLc×d\mathbf{Q}_{c}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{L_{c}\times d} be the query matrix for the current chunk cc;
𝐊i,𝐕i∈ℝLc×d\mathbf{K}_{i},\mathbf{V}_{i}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{L_{c}\times d} be keys/values for KV-chunk i≤ci\leq c (context up to and including cc);
𝐘left∈ℝLc×d\mathbf{Y}_{\text{left}}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{L_{c}\times d} be the accumulated softmax-weighted numerators from prior chunks; and
𝐥left∈ℝLc×1\mathbf{l}_{\text{left}}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{L_{c}\times 1} be the corresponding accumulated denominators.
These accumulators enable numerically correct, memory-efficient incremental attention across chunks, well-suited to tiled NPUs.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS3.p5.1] For clarity, we consider full causal attention for a single KV head (i.e., without GQA). At each chunk step, attention is computed as follows:
[id=S3.I1.i1] 1.
[id=S3.I1.i1.p1.1] Attention Score Computation:
[id=S3.E6]
𝐒c=𝐐c​𝐊c⊤/d\mathbf{S}_{c}={\mathbf{Q}_{c}\mathbf{K}_{c}^{\top}}/{\sqrt{d}}
(6)
[id=S3.I1.i1.p1.2] where 𝐒c∈ℝLc×Lc\mathbf{S}_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{c}\times L_{c}} contains the raw attention scores between current queries and keys in this chunk.
[id=S3.I1.i2] 2.
[id=S3.I1.i2.p1.1] Numerical Stabilization:
[id=S3.E7]
𝐦c=max⁡(𝐒c,𝐦cleft)\mathbf{m}_{c}=\max(\mathbf{S}_{c},\mathbf{m}_{c}^{\text{left}})
(7)
[id=S3.I1.i2.p1.2] where 𝐦c,𝐦cleft∈ℝLc×1\mathbf{m}_{c},\mathbf{m}_{c}^{\text{left}}\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{c}\times 1} are row-wise max values across current and previous chunks.
[id=S3.I1.i3] 3.
[id=S3.I1.i3.p1.1] Exponentiation with Shift:
[id=S3.E8]
𝐅c=exp⁡(𝐒c−𝐦c)\mathbf{F}_{c}=\exp(\mathbf{S}_{c}-\mathbf{m}_{c})
(8)
[id=S3.I1.i3.p1.2] where 𝐅c∈ℝLc×Lc\mathbf{F}_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{c}\times L_{c}} contains the softmax numerators.
[id=S3.I1.i4] 4.
[id=S3.I1.i4.p1.1] Correction Factor for Previous Chunks:
[id=S3.E9]
𝐂c=exp⁡(𝐦cleft−𝐦c)\mathbf{C}_{c}=\exp(\mathbf{m}_{c}^{\text{left}}-\mathbf{m}_{c})
(9)
[id=S3.I1.i4.p1.2] where 𝐂c∈ℝLc×1\mathbf{C}_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{c}\times 1} ensures proper scaling when combining current and prior accumulations.
[id=S3.I1.i5] 5.
[id=S3.I1.i5.p1.1] Accumulate Softmax Denominator:
[id=S3.E10]
𝐥=𝐂c​⨀𝐥left+∑𝐅c(row-wise sum)\mathbf{l}=\mathbf{C}_{c}\bigodot\mathbf{l}_{\text{left}}+\sum\mathbf{F}_{c}\quad\text{(row-wise sum)}
(10)
[id=S3.I1.i5.p1.2] where 𝐥,𝐥left∈ℝLc×1\mathbf{l},\mathbf{l}_{\text{left}}\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{c}\times 1} represent the running softmax denominator across all chunks seen so far.
[id=S3.I1.i6] 6.
[id=S3.I1.i6.p1.1] Accumulate Softmax-Weighted Values:
[id=S3.E11]
𝐘=𝐂c​⨀𝐘left+𝐅c​𝐕c\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{C}_{c}\bigodot\mathbf{Y}_{\text{left}}+\mathbf{F}_{c}\mathbf{V}_{c}
(11)
[id=S3.I1.i6.p1.2] where 𝐘,𝐘left∈ℝLc×d\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Y}_{\text{left}}\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{c}\times d} accumulate the weighted value vectors across chunks.
[id=S3.I1.i7] 7.
[id=S3.I1.i7.p1.1] Final Attention Output (after all chunks):
[id=S3.E12]
𝐎=𝐘/𝐥\mathbf{O}=\mathbf{Y}/\mathbf{l}
(12)
[id=S3.I1.i7.p1.2] where 𝐎∈ℝLc×d\mathbf{O}\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{c}\times d} is the final attention output for the current query chunk.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS3.p7.1] This chunked attention approach, illustrated in Fig. 7, offers several key advantages critical for efficient execution on hardware-constrained platforms like AMD Ryzen AI NPUs:
Figure 7:
Illustration of the chunked attention workflow. Processing proceeds strictly from left to right, as indicated by the red arrow, to preserve causal attention. Chunks along the diagonal contain only lower triangular regions, reflecting the causal constraint that tokens cannot attend to future positions. Each chunk operation requires the corresponding 𝐐\mathbf{Q}, 𝐊\mathbf{K}, and 𝐕\mathbf{V} blocks (e.g., 𝐐𝟐\mathbf{Q_{2}}, 𝐊𝟏\mathbf{K_{1}}, and 𝐕𝟏\mathbf{V_{1}} here), as well as the intermediate values 𝐦cleft\mathbf{m}_{c}^{\text{left}}, 𝐥left\mathbf{l}_{\text{left}}, and 𝐘left\mathbf{Y}_{\text{left}} passed from the preceding (left) chunk.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS3.p8.1] In chunked attention, causality is preserved by allowing each query in the current chunk to attend to all K/V from the current and all prior chunks, with a causal mask (diagonal or end-chunk per process) as in Fig. 7; memory remains bounded by keeping only the running accumulations 𝐘left\mathbf{Y}_{\text{left}} and 𝐥left\mathbf{l}_{\text{left}} instead of full softmax numerators/denominators; and hardware efficiency is achieved via chunkwise tiling that fits each attention block within a compute tile (CT) and uses double-buffered DMA to overlap transfer and compute, maximizing throughput.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS3.p9.1] As shown in Fig. 8, FlowQKV maps cleanly to the NPU: Gemma3-4B (text) uses 4 KV groups, each serving 2 query heads. Each KV group is handled by 2 adjacent CTs in a col. Queries run in chunks–2 CT columns per Q-chunk–so 8 columns cover 4 chunks (a super chunk; see Fig. 7).
Figure 8:
Illustration of FlowQKV execution on an NPU, showing 2 CT columns for Q0Q_{0} chunk.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS3.p10.1] KK, VV chunks (𝐐c\mathbf{Q}_{c}) are loaded into the CTs via two parallel DMA channels, while QQ chunks is broadcast to all CTs. Each CT then selects the relevant portion of the QQ heads it needs for computation. This enables simultaneous data transfer. For each set of query chunks, a KV chunk sweep is performed, where the queries are evaluated against all available KV chunks to compute the attention output. After this sweep completes, the next group of query chunks can be processed. In causal attention (this example), the sweep must span progressively more chunks (or super-chunks) as the context grows. FlowQKV enables attention computation to scale to long contexts with high efficiency, leveraging Ryzen AI’s tiled compute architecture and bandwidth hierarchy.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS3.p11.1] We can use Eq. 13 to measure the Umemr​dU_{\text{mem}}^{rd} in runtime. TdT_{d} denotes the total measured runtime over prefill sequence length (LL). This captures the quadratic O⁡(L2)O(L^{2}) behavior related to attention’s inherent complexity.
[id=S3.E13]
Umemr​d=2​B⋅(1+LLc)⋅L⋅CTcount⋅HTdU_{\text{mem}}^{rd}=\frac{2B\cdot\bigl(1+\tfrac{L}{L_{c}}\bigr)\cdot L\cdot\mathrm{CT}_{\mathrm{count}}\cdot H}{T_{d}}
(13)
[id=S3.SS1.SSS3.p13.1] A higher Umemr​dU_{\text{mem}}^{rd} indicates better utilization of the available memory bandwidth. Optimizing FlowQKV to maximize Umemr​dU_{\text{mem}}^{rd} ensures the design is memory-bound (peak efficiency). This metric is used assess the impact of various tile configurations and scheduling strategies on hardware performance.
[id=S3.SS1.SSS3.p14.1] FlowQKV has two variants: FlowQKV-SWA (for local layers), which restricts the chunk sweep to a sliding window (Lc=1024)(L_{c}=1024), and FlowQKV-NCA (non-causal for ViT), which sweeps the full sequence. FlowQKV, FlowQKV-SWA, and FlowQKV-NCA share the same hardware configuration; only the instruction schedules differ.

3.2 Decoding
[id=S3.SS2.p1.1] The core computations in LLM decoding—projection and attention—are both memory-bound, meaning their performance is limited by Umemr​dU_{\text{mem}}^{rd}. Maximum throughput is achieved when this bandwidth is saturated.
[id=S3.SS2.SSS1]
3.2.1 FusedDQP (Fused dequantization and projection)
[id=S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1] We describe the MVM operation as
[id=S3.E14]
𝐘=𝐖×𝐀,\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{W}\times\mathbf{A},
(14)
[id=S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.2] where 𝐖∈ℝM×K\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times K} is the projection matrix and 𝐀∈ℝK×1\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times 1} is the input activation vector.
[id=S3.SS2.SSS1.p2.1] We tile 𝐖\mathbf{W} into smaller blocks of size m×k=32×256m\times k=32\times 256 (Fig. 9), denoted as 𝐰\mathbf{w}, which matches the quantization block size. Similarly, 𝐀\mathbf{A} is divided into small vectors 𝐚∈ℝk×1\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times 1}, with k=256k=256 chosen to align with Q4NX quantization. This naturally partitions the output 𝐘\mathbf{Y} into tiles 𝐲∈ℝm×1\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times 1}. In the single compute tile (CT) scenario, the first vector 𝐚\mathbf{a} is loaded into the CT, and accumulation proceeds via:
[id=S3.E15]
𝐲acc+=dequant​(𝐰)×𝐚\mathbf{y}_{\text{acc}}\mathrel{+}=\text{dequant}(\mathbf{w})\times\mathbf{a}
(15)
[id=S3.SS2.SSS1.p3.1] Importantly, the dequantization in Eq. 15 does not operate on the entire 𝐰\mathbf{w} block at once. Instead, 𝐰\mathbf{w} is further partitioned into fine-grained sub-blocks of size 16×816\times 8, which are streamed into vector processor. For each sub-block, dequantization and MVM are executed in a fused kernel, involving only one load from and one store to L1 memory. This fusion maximizes register reuse and minimizes memory access overhead.
[id=S3.SS2.SSS1.p4.1] Once a 𝐰\mathbf{w} is fully used, subsequent 𝐚\mathbf{a} vectors and their corresponding 𝐰\mathbf{w} blocks (to the right of the previous 𝐰\mathbf{w}) are fetched and processed until the full 𝐲acc\mathbf{y}_{\text{acc}} is computed (Fig. 9). When multiple CTs are used, the vector 𝐚\mathbf{a} is broadcast to all CTs. Each CT independently fetches its associated quantized 𝐰\mathbf{w} block from DRAM and performs MVM in parallel.

3.2.2 FlowKV
[id=S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1] FlowKV is an hardware-aware attention scheme that optimizes KV-cache access to maximize DRAM bandwidth.
[id=S3.SS2.SSS2.p2.1] During LLM decoding, the full KV cache grows with sequence length, creating pressure on memory bandwidth and on-chip storage. To mitigate this, we adopt a chunk-wise processing approach: the sequence is divided into chunks of size LcL_{c}, and the NPU processes one chunk at a time. Assuming GQA, each KV head is shared by H/GH/G query heads. As an example, consider single-head causal full attention. The equations are similar to FlowQKV in prefill (Sec. 3.1.3), except that the Q chunk size is 1 during decoding.
[id=S3.SS2.SSS3]
3.2.3 Efficient Mapping to the NPU
[id=S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.1] As shown in Fig. 10, two CTs are used to implement the FlowKV attention pipeline. CT0 handles steps (1)–(5) of the FlowKV procedure (Sec. 3.1.3). CT1 performs steps (6)–(7). Intermediate results (FF, CC, and ll) are passed directly from CT0 to CT1 via AIE on-chip memory (green arrow in Fig. 10). Both key and value chunks are streamed into the CTs using double buffering.
Figure 10: FlowKV pipeline (2-CT scenario): CT0 streams in key chunks to compute attention scores and passes intermediate results (FF, CC, LL) to CT1. CT1 streams in value chunks and performs softmax-weighted accumulation to produce the final output. This pipeline enables concurrent key and value processing, maximizing NPU bandwidth utilization.
[id=S3.SS2.SSS3.p2.1] Ideally, the computation latency for each chunk overlaps with its transfer time, effectively hiding kernel execution overhead, illustrated in Fig. 11. While Fig. 10 illustrates a 2-CT example, the design is flexible: the chunk size LcL_{c}, number of CTs, or number of KV heads can be adjusted to data transfer time and compute intensity towards ideal case to achieve the best performance.
[id=S3.SS2.SSS3.p3.1] Two CT columns (8 CTs) are assigned to the FlowKV kernel. In this configuration, every two CTs operate as a pair (as illustrated in Fig. 10). Thus, a total of 4 pairs are formed. One KV head (a group) mapped to each CT pair. This mapping balances the chunk data transfer time with kernel execution latency, enabling efficient pipelined execution across the CTs and maximizing Umemr​dU_{\text{mem}}^{rd}. For projection operations, four CT columns (16 CTs) to the FusedDQP kernel. One CT is dedicated to each of the nonlinear operations: RoPE, RMS normalization with residual connection, and GeLU activation with MUL (Fig. 4). These functions operate on vector inputs, which are temporarily stored in MTs between compute stages. All nonlinear kernels are fully pipelined, and their execution incurs negligible latency compared to projection and attention operations during LLM decoding.
Figure 11: Timing diagram of the FlowKV pipeline (2-CT configuration) under ideal conditions, where data transfer is fully overlapped with kernel execution in both CTs.
[id=S3.SS2.SSS3.p4.1] FlowKV has 1 variant: FlowKV-SWA (for local layers), which limits the chunk sweep to a sliding window (Lc=1024L_{c}=1024). FlowKV and FlowKV-SWA share the same hardware configuration; only the instruction differs.

5 Discussion
[id=S5.p1.1] Integrated NPUs are designed for low-power, privacy-preserving, always-on edge scenarios such as laptops and handheld devices, rather than multi-tenant datacenter workloads or very large models; they are not intended to compete directly with discrete or datacenter GPUs in that regime.
[id=S5.p2.1] The proposed method executes unmodified LLMs, preserving full model accuracy without any algorithmic changes. For MM, FusedDQP (and its variants), and FlowKV/FlowQKV (and their variants), the theoretical sustained read bandwidth requirement UmemrdU_{\text{mem}}^{\mathrm{rd}} exceeds 60​GB/s60\,\mathrm{GB/s} at 1.8​GHz1.8\,\mathrm{GHz} and scales linearly with clock frequency. A system is memory-bound when the vendor-allocated NPU read bandwidth is lower than UmemrdU_{\text{mem}}^{\mathrm{rd}}; otherwise it is compute-bound.
[id=S5.p3.1] On the test chip, the NPU’s read memory bandwidth is capped below 40​GB/s40\,\mathrm{GB/s}, so these kernels operate in the memory-bound regime. The CPU and iGPU get far more memory bandwidth, which explains their decoding speed advantage at short contexts. Under sufficient bandwidth, MM, FusedDQP, FlowKV/FlowQKV scale linearly with the number of compute tiles (CTs). As future NPUs provide higher memory bandwidth and more CTs, they are expected to substantially outperform CPU- and iGPU-based solutions in both speed and efficiency.
[id=S5.p4.1] We are also developing and maturing toolchains and libraries to accelerate LLM deployment on the NPU chips; these will be released in the near future.
[id=S5.p5.1] Although demonstrated on AMD Ryzen AI NPUs, we believe the techniques generalize to dataflow-style accelerators with tiled compute, local SRAM, and DMA or broadcast, and can be adapted to platforms such as Cerebras, and AMD AIE/ACAP, etc.

6 Conclusion
[id=S6.p1.1] We demonstrate the first end-to-end mapping of Gemma3 text–vision models onto a tiled edge NPU (AMD Ryzen AI NPU), showing that hardware-aware scheduling and bandwidth-centric kernels enable efficient, accurate, low-power inference without algorithmic changes. FlowQKV and FlowKV sustain high DRAM utilization for attention, FusedDQP removes projection overheads, and the compact Q4NX format reduces memory footprint while preserving fidelity. On Ryzen AI, these techniques yield multi-×\times speedups and up to 200×200\times+ power-efficiency gains over CPU/iGPU baselines. The principles generalize to future NPUs and other dataflow accelerators, enabling scalable, real-time LLM/VLM inference at the edge.
